words.definition: An amount far greater than what is needed or can be used.
words.example: The new intern was overwhelmed by a plethora of logins, badges, and forms on her first day.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'PLENTY-thora' — plenty, and then a whole lot more.

words.definition: An excessive amount, especially of food or drink, causing discomfort.
words.example: After the holidays, a surfeit of rich food left him queasy and sluggish for a week.
words.mnemonic: 'SUR-' means over (like surplus) + 'feit' — you're so over-full you can't fit into your clothes.

words.definition: A supply so large that it exceeds demand and drives down value.
words.example: A glut of avocados flooded the market, and prices dropped to almost nothing.
words.mnemonic: 'Glut' lives inside 'glutton' — a glutton overeats, a market glut is overstuffed.

words.definition: A very large quantity of something, spread out lavishly.
words.example: In spring the meadow bursts into a profusion of wildflowers in every color.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'profundere', to pour forth — say 'pro-FUSE' and picture color pouring out everywhere.

words.definition: A horn-shaped emblem overflowing with fruit that symbolizes a rich, plentiful supply.
words.example: The farmers' market in autumn was a cornucopia of squash, apples, and fresh-baked bread.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'cornu' (horn) + 'copia' (plenty): literally the 'horn of plenty' tipping over with fruit.

words.definition: The state of having a great deal of money and material wealth.
words.example: The gated neighborhood, with its manicured lawns and imported cars, radiated quiet affluence.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'a-FLU-ence' — from Latin 'fluere', to flow: money flows steadily toward you.

words.definition: Great luxury, richness, and lavish display of wealth.
words.example: Gold ceilings and crystal chandeliers gave the ballroom an air of dizzying opulence.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'opal-ence' — imagine every room studded with glittering opals and jewels.

words.definition: A full or complete amount; a great supply.
words.example: The library offered a plenitude of resources, from rare manuscripts to online archives.
words.mnemonic: 'Plen-' (Latin 'plenus', full) + '-itude' — the quality of being brim-full.

words.definition: A generous, plentiful yield or gift, especially from nature or a harvest.
words.example: The autumn harvest gave them a bounty of pumpkins, corn, and crisp apples.
words.mnemonic: Root 'bon' means good (Latin 'bonus') — a bounty is a heap of good things given freely.

words.definition: An amount beyond what is needed or useful; a needless extra.
words.example: The report was padded with a superfluity of charts nobody actually read.
words.mnemonic: 'Super' (over) + 'fluere' (flow) — so much it flows over the top and spills to waste.

words.definition: A very large quantity; more than enough of something.
words.example: After the rains, the region enjoyed an abundance of clean water for the first time in years.
words.mnemonic: Picture 'a bun dance' — so many buns they're dancing across the table.

words.definition: A large enough amount to fully meet a need.
words.example: Don't worry about running out — there's plenty of soup for everyone.
words.mnemonic: 'Plen-' from Latin 'plenus', full; it also rhymes with 'twenty' — picture twenty of everything.

words.definition: Large in amount or number; present in great quantity.
words.example: She took copious notes during the lecture, filling three notebooks by the end.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'copy-us' — imagine a photocopier spitting out endless copies.

words.definition: Existing in large amounts; more than enough.
words.example: Fish were so plentiful in the bay that nets came up full within minutes.
words.mnemonic: Read it as 'plenty + full' — full of plenty.

words.definition: Present in large amounts, or freely giving much to others.
words.example: The bountiful harvest filled every barn on the farm and still left grain to spare.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'bounty-full' — a treasure chest crammed full of bounty.

words.definition: Generous in giving, or supplied in large amounts.
words.example: Their bounteous host kept refilling plates until no guest could eat another bite.
words.mnemonic: 'Bounty' + '-eous' — a giver so full of bounty it feels beauteous.

words.definition: Existing in great abundance; more than enough.
words.example: After the rains, water was plenteous, and the wells never ran dry that summer.
words.mnemonic: 'Plenty' + '-eous' — so much on hand there's plenty for everyone.

words.definition: Completely filled or well stocked with something.
words.example: The museum's archive was replete with letters, maps, and photographs from every decade.
words.mnemonic: 'Re-PLETE' echoes 'complete' — filled right up to completion.

words.definition: Swarming or crowded with a large number of things.
words.example: The tide pool was teeming with crabs, snails, and darting silver fish.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'teaming' up — countless creatures forming one huge team.

words.definition: Widespread and common, often referring to something unwelcome.
words.example: Rumors were rife in the office after the sudden resignation of the director.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'life' — trouble so common it becomes a way of life.

words.definition: Showing great wealth, luxury, or richness.
words.example: The opulent ballroom glittered with gold chandeliers, silk drapes, and marble floors.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'opal-lent' — a place dripping with opals and jewels.

words.definition: Spending or given generously, often in an extravagant way.
words.example: She threw a lavish party with a five-course dinner and a live orchestra.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'ravish' — spending so extravagantly it dazzles the eye.

words.definition: Splendid and costly-looking; richly luxurious.
words.example: The hotel served a sumptuous breakfast of fresh pastries, smoked salmon, and tropical fruit.
words.mnemonic: Hear the 'sum' — a huge sum was spent to make it this grand.

words.definition: Spending money or resources recklessly and wastefully.
words.example: His prodigal habits drained the inheritance within a single reckless year.
words.mnemonic: The 'Prodigal Son' squandered his whole fortune — prodigal means wildly wasteful.

words.definition: Overflowing with lively energy, excitement, and high spirits.
words.example: The children were exuberant, racing and laughing across the yard on the last day of school.
words.mnemonic: 'Ex-uber-ant' — an 'uber' amount of enthusiasm bursting right out.

words.definition: Growing thickly and abundantly; lush and rich.
words.example: Luxuriant vines covered the old cottage, their leaves so dense the walls vanished.
words.mnemonic: 'Luxury-plant' — foliage growing in thick, lush, over-the-top abundance.

words.definition: Producing many works, offspring, or results in great numbers.
words.example: The prolific author published three novels and dozens of short stories in one decade.
words.mnemonic: 'Pro-life-ic' — a pro at churning out life or output nonstop.

words.definition: Able to produce abundant crops, offspring, or ideas.
words.example: The fertile valley grew everything from wheat to grapes without much irrigation.
words.mnemonic: Same root as 'fertilizer' — what you add to make land produce.

words.definition: Producing plentiful positive results or achievements.
words.example: Their weekend brainstorming session was fruitful, generating five ideas the team actually launched.
words.mnemonic: A tree heavy with fruit yields a rich harvest — full of fruit, full of results.

words.definition: Impressively enormous in size, amount, or degree.
words.example: The young pianist showed a prodigious talent, memorizing entire symphonies at age six.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'prodigy' — a child prodigy has prodigious gifts.

words.definition: More than enough for what is needed.
words.example: The hall had ample seating, so nobody had to stand during the lecture.
words.mnemonic: Ample rhymes with 'sample' — there's enough for everyone to sample and plenty left.

words.definition: Beyond what is needed; serving no useful purpose.
words.example: Once the summary said it all, the extra ten slides felt superfluous.
words.mnemonic: Super + fluous (flow) — an extra flow that spills over past what's required.

words.definition: Present in very large quantities; plentiful.
words.example: Rain was abundant that spring, and the reservoirs overflowed for months.
words.mnemonic: A-BUN-dant — picture a bakery with a bun for everyone and thousands still left.

words.definition: Consisting of countless or very many elements.
words.example: From the hilltop we saw a myriad of city lights flickering below.
words.mnemonic: Myriad sounds like 'my riot' — a riot of too many things to count.

words.definition: Many and varied in kind or number.
words.example: Her reasons for leaving were manifold, ranging from money to family to health.
words.mnemonic: Many + fold — folded over again and again into many different kinds.

words.definition: Extremely numerous; existing in great numbers.
words.example: The multitudinous stars scattered across the desert sky defied any attempt to count them.
words.mnemonic: Hidden inside is 'multitude' — a multitude of things is multitudinous.

words.definition: To exist in great numbers or amounts.
words.example: Rumors abound whenever a celebrity cancels an appearance without explanation.
words.mnemonic: A + BOUND — imagine things leaping and bounding around everywhere in swarms.

words.definition: To fill or soak something completely until no more fits.
words.example: The heavy rain saturated the field, leaving mud that squelched with every step.
words.mnemonic: SAT-urate — think of a sponge that 'sat' in a bucket until it could hold no more.

words.definition: To overwhelm someone or something with a very large amount.
words.example: After the ad aired, calls inundated the switchboard and operators couldn't keep up.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'unda' (wave) — waves come flooding IN, one after another.

words.definition: A great flood or an overwhelming rush of something.
words.example: The post went viral, and a deluge of emails buried her inbox overnight.
words.mnemonic: Deluge sounds like 'the luge' — picture water sledding downhill in an unstoppable torrent.

words.definition: To swell or fill up with fluid, often to bursting.
words.example: The leech engorged itself with blood until it was three times its normal size.
words.mnemonic: EN + GORGE — to gorge and stuff something until it swells fat.

words.definition: To satisfy an appetite or desire completely.
words.example: The enormous holiday feast finally satiated even the hungriest guests at the table.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'say she ate' — she ate until fully satisfied and could take no more.

words.definition: To fill someone completely with food or pleasure until no more is wanted.
words.example: After three helpings of stew, the hikers were finally sated and pushed their bowls away.
words.mnemonic: Ends in 'ate' — once you've truly ATE enough, you are sate-d.

words.definition: To cause disgust by being far too sweet, rich, or sentimental.
words.example: The frosting was pleasant at first, but by the third cupcake its sweetness began to cloy.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'ahoy' — too much sugary 'oy!' makes your stomach turn.

words.definition: To be filled all the way up to the very edge.
words.example: Her eyes began to brim with tears the moment the letter mentioned home.
words.mnemonic: Think of a hat's BRIM — the top edge; liquid reaches that line.

words.definition: To spill over the top because a container holds more than it can keep.
words.example: She forgot the running tap, and soon water began to overflow onto the kitchen floor.
words.mnemonic: OVER + FLOW — the liquid literally flows over the top.

words.definition: To fill a supply back up after some of it has been used.
words.example: Every autumn the squirrels rush to replenish their winter store of acorns.
words.mnemonic: RE- (again) + 'plenish' like 'plenty' — make it plenty once more.

words.definition: To move or gather in a large, dense, restless crowd.
words.example: Fans began to swarm the stage the instant the band walked off.
words.mnemonic: SWARM sounds like a 'warm' buzz of bees pressing together.

words.definition: To eat something eagerly in very large amounts.
words.example: The children would gorge on candy every Halloween until they felt sick.
words.mnemonic: Your GORGE is your throat (old meaning) — you stuff it when you overeat.

words.definition: A person who habitually eats and drinks far too much.
words.example: Such a glutton was he that he ordered a second dinner before finishing the first.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'glut' — a glut is an oversupply, and this person craves an oversupply of food.

words.definition: Given to eating and drinking far more than the body needs.
words.example: His gluttonous habit of clearing every buffet tray left little for anyone else.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'glut' inside it — a glut, or excess, of eating.

words.definition: Wanting huge amounts of food, or eager for a great deal of something.
words.example: A voracious reader, she finished four thick novels over a single weekend.
words.mnemonic: Shares 'vor' with 'deVOUR' (Latin vorare, to swallow whole).

words.definition: Aggressively grasping for far more money or goods than one needs.
words.example: The rapacious landlord kept raising rents until half the tenants were forced out.
words.mnemonic: Shares 'rap' with 'rapture' — Latin rapere, to seize or snatch away.

words.definition: Impossible to satisfy, no matter how much is given.
words.example: Her insatiable curiosity meant every answer only led her to ten new questions.
words.mnemonic: IN- (not) + 'satiable' from 'satisfy' — it can never be satisfied.

words.definition: Extremely eager to gain and hoard money.
words.example: The avaricious banker counted his coins twice nightly and gave nothing to charity.
words.mnemonic: Say 'a-VARI-cious' — picture a miser hungry for VARIous piles of gold.

words.definition: An extreme desire to pile up and keep wealth.
words.example: Blinded by avarice, he betrayed his oldest friend for a share of the treasure.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'have-a-rich' — the endless drive to have riches.

words.definition: A strong, selfish craving for money and possessions.
words.example: The auctioneer played on the crowd's cupidity, and bids climbed far past reason.
words.mnemonic: Looks like 'Cupid,' but this longing is for cash, not love.

words.definition: Marked by a strong, envious longing for what other people possess.
words.example: He cast a covetous glance at his neighbor's gleaming new sports car.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'covet us' — someone eyeing what's ours and aching to have it.

words.definition: To wish enviously to own something that belongs to another person.
words.example: She had quietly coveted the corner office with its river view for years.
words.mnemonic: Break it into 'co-vet': two vets both wanting the same rare pet.

words.definition: Keenly eager to obtain and keep money or possessions.
words.example: His acquisitive nature filled the house with objects he never once used.
words.mnemonic: Rooted in 'acquire' — an acquisitive person is always out to acquire more.

words.definition: To secretly store up a large supply, often far more than needed.
words.example: During the shortage, some families hoarded canned food in their basements.
words.mnemonic: Homophone of 'horde' — picture a horde of stuff piled up in a hidden stash.

words.definition: To gather together a great quantity of something over time.
words.example: Over the decades she amassed one of the world's finest stamp collections.
words.mnemonic: A + MASS: you build up a growing mass of something.

words.definition: To build up gradually, especially as interest or added benefit.
words.example: Interest accrues on the loan every month until the balance is repaid.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a crew' that keeps swelling as more hands sign on.

words.definition: To collect a growing amount of something little by little.
words.example: Dust had accumulated on the shelves during the long summer vacation.
words.mnemonic: Think of a 'cumulus' cloud that grows by piling up more and more.

words.definition: To combine separate items into one collected mass or total.
words.example: The website aggregates headlines from hundreds of sources onto a single page.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'grex' (flock) — you herd a scattered flock into one group.

words.definition: Slow growth or increase caused by the gradual addition of layers.
words.example: The coral reef expanded through the steady accretion of tiny skeletons.
words.mnemonic: Related to 'concrete' setting — matter hardening on, layer by layer.

words.definition: A condition of not having enough to meet demand.
words.example: Water scarcity turned the once-green fields into cracked, dusty earth.
words.mnemonic: Built from 'scarce'; it also sounds like 'scare' — it's scary when supplies run dry.

words.definition: The state of being extremely poor and without resources.
words.example: After the business collapsed, the family lived in penury for years.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'penny-ury' — scraping by on your very last penny.

words.definition: A condition of severe poverty and constant material want.
words.example: The charity was founded to relieve the indigence of the city's poorest residents.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'in dig' — so broke you're digging in the dirt for scraps.

words.definition: A state of lacking essential things like food, shelter, or comfort.
words.example: The refugees endured months of privation, surviving on scraps and sleeping in the cold.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'deprived nation' — a nation stripped of basics lives in privation.

words.definition: A lack of something necessary for health, function, or completeness.
words.example: A vitamin D deficiency left her bones weak and prone to fracture.
words.mnemonic: De-FISH-ency — picture a fish tank drained of water; something essential is missing.

words.definition: The amount by which money spent exceeds money earned or available.
words.example: The government ran a huge deficit after spending far more than it collected in taxes.
words.mnemonic: DEF-i-sit — the budget can't 'sit' level; a definite gap tips it over.

words.definition: A situation where the available supply falls below what people need.
words.example: A water shortage during the drought forced the town to ration every drop.
words.mnemonic: SHORT + age — an age when things run short and the shelves go empty.

words.definition: The condition of not having enough of what is required.
words.example: Cardiac insufficiency meant his heart could no longer pump enough blood to his limbs.
words.mnemonic: In (not) + 'suffice' — when something does not suffice, you face insufficiency.

words.definition: An extreme and widespread scarcity of food across a region.
words.example: The failed harvest brought a famine that claimed thousands of lives that winter.
words.mnemonic: FAM-ine — a whole 'family' left famished with nothing to eat.

words.definition: The quality of being careful and sparing with money or resources.
words.example: Her frugality was legendary; she darned socks for years rather than buy new ones.
words.mnemonic: FRU-gal — 'a gal who saves every fruit' and lets nothing go to waste.

words.definition: Extreme unwillingness to spend money or use resources; stinginess.
words.example: His parsimony was so severe he reused tea bags and refused to heat the house.
words.mnemonic: PARSE-money — someone who 'parses' every coin, splitting hairs over cash.

words.definition: Careful management of money and the avoidance of waste.
words.example: Through years of thrift she saved enough to buy the cottage outright.
words.mnemonic: THRIFT store — where careful savers shop to stretch every dollar.

words.definition: The state of lacking or being denied basic needs or benefits.
words.example: Sleep deprivation left the new parents dazed and unable to concentrate.
words.mnemonic: De-PRIVE — to 'pry' something away; what's pried loose becomes your deprivation.

words.definition: A lack or absence of something needed or desired.
words.example: For want of a nail the shoe was lost, and for want of a shoe the kingdom fell.
words.mnemonic: WANT — the thing you 'want' is precisely the thing you are missing.

words.definition: Barely enough; very small in amount or degree.
words.example: They paid scant attention to the warnings and pressed on into the storm.
words.mnemonic: SCANT rhymes with 'can't' — there's so little you can't get by on it.

words.definition: Too small or limited in amount to be adequate.
words.example: The hikers rationed their scanty supply of water, unsure when they'd find more.
words.mnemonic: SCANTY — 'scant' plus -y; a scanty outfit barely covers anything.

words.definition: Small in amount and clearly not enough.
words.example: He tried to stretch his meager wages across a whole month of rent and food.
words.mnemonic: MEAGER sounds like 'meek ogre' — even an ogre turns meek on such tiny portions.

words.definition: Thinly scattered or present in only small amounts across an area.
words.example: Only a handful of houses dotted the sparse settlement along the desert highway.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'spare' — when you can only spare a little, there's very little around.
